claims.text: Thermodynamically favorable entropic mixing promotes solid-solution formation in rapidly processed noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Kinetically limited atomic diffusion competes with entropic mixing and governs solid-solution formation.
Rapid processing provides insufficient diffusion time for all constituent elements to mix uniformly.
Differences in intrinsic atomic mobility and diffusion barriers cause local elemental segregation and phase separation.
Extending the dwell time at a critical intermediate temperature increases elemental diffusion.
The increased diffusion produced by an extended dwell enhances uniform nucleation and stabilizes a single-phase solid solution.
Rapidly synthesized noble metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles often exhibit uncontrolled morphology, phase separation, and elemental segregation because of insufficient diffusion.
An extended intermediate-temperature dwell can provide additional diffusion time without significant particle coarsening or thermal decomposition.
The intervention is expected to work when constituent atomic-size mismatches are modest, described as typically below 5–10%.
The degree of atomic-scale mixing during nucleation is modulated by the diffusion length of each element under the imposed thermal profile.
Rapid heating reaches temperatures at which thermodynamic mixing is favored.
A short time at high temperature limits atomic diffusion.
Rapid cooling freezes locally segregated clusters into the nanoparticles.
An extended intermediate-temperature dwell permits diffusion to homogenize the elemental distribution.
A homogenized elemental distribution promotes nucleation of a uniform single-phase solid solution.
Compared with rapid heating and cooling alone, an extended dwell will produce a more uniform elemental distribution.
Compared with the baseline, an extended dwell will reduce phase segregation and increase the prevalence of the targeted single-phase crystal structure.
The intervention is applicable only when dwell time can be increased without excessive grain growth or thermal decomposition.
The intervention is more applicable to compositions whose constituent elements have similar diffusion coefficients and moderate atomic-size mismatches.
The intervention may not improve structure selection when atomic-size mismatches are very high or the baseline process already provides ample atomic mobility.
